item.title: Fugu Preparation Class in Shimonoseki — Guide
item.description: Because fugu can be lethal if prepared wrongly, only chefs with a special licence earned through rigorous training and examination may handle and serve it — and in Shimonoseki, the heart of Japan’s fugu trade, some venues let curious visitors get a hands-on glimpse of that craft. A fugu preparation experience typically involves watching or trying, under close expert supervision, how the fish is cleaned, how its toxic parts are carefully removed and set aside, and how the flesh is sliced into the famous wafer-thin sashimi — before, of course, eating the results.

item.title: Shimonoseki Aquarium (Kaikyokan) — Guide
item.description: The Shimonoseki Marine Science Museum, known as Kaikyokan, is one of western Japan’s most enjoyable aquariums, set right on the Kanmon Strait waterfront beside the Karato area. Fitting for a city built on blowfish, it is famous for the world’s largest collection of fugu and pufferfish species, displayed alongside a huge blue whale skeleton, a lively dolphin and sea lion show, penguins in a large habitat, and tanks recreating the marine life of the strait itself.

item.title: Shimonoseki Fugu: Eating Blowfish in Its Capital — Guide
item.description: Shimonoseki is the fugu capital of Japan, landing the great majority of the nation’s blowfish and treating it as the city’s signature delicacy. Fugu is famous as much for its danger as its taste — parts of the fish are highly poisonous, so only specially licensed chefs may prepare it — but in expert hands it is utterly safe and prized for its clean, delicate flavour and firm texture. The classic way to eat it is ‘fugu sashi’, wafer-thin translucent slices arranged like petals, followed by ‘fugu-chiri’ hotpot, deep-fried karaage, and grilled fin sake.
